How did humans discover fire? Gold? Why do we wear rings, fear the dark, or crave sugar?

How America got electricity — and who paid for it.

Kilowatt Nation tells the story of the American power grid through the people who built it, the money and deals that shaped it, and the nights it failed. Rural electrification and the farm cooperatives that strung their own lines. The utility empires, the men who ran them, and the bargains that decided who owns the wire outside your house. The great blackouts — 1965, New York in 1977, the Northeast in 2003, Texas in 2021 — reconstructed minute by minute from official reports, archival photographs and the accounts of those on shift.

Every episode is a long-form documentary on American electrical infrastructure and industrial history: power plants, dams, transmission lines, substations and the companies behind them, from the first city systems of the 1880s to the grid we depend on now. Sourced from public archives and government investigations, told for anyone who has worked in this industry — or lost power because of it.

Gold is one of the strangest things humans have ever become obsessed with.

It’s too soft to make a good weapon. It’s too heavy to carry in large quantities. You can’t eat it, build a shelter with it, or use it to grow food. And yet, for roughly 7,000 years, humans have dug it from the ground, buried it with their dead, turned it into crowns and jewelry, fought over it, used it as money, and built entire economic systems around it.

So why gold?

.

Why have humans always been obsessed with gold?
